claims.text: The starting material consists of crystalline, near-equiatomic, single-solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least five metals.
Introducing a sacrificial oxide surface layer can overcome structural or chemical instability in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilizing intervention is the introduction of a sacrificial oxide layer.
The sacrificial oxide layer protects the underlying alloy nanoparticles from oxidation.
The sacrificial oxide layer protects the underlying alloy nanoparticles from corrosion.
Protection from oxidation and corrosion preserves nanoparticle structural stability.
Protection from oxidation and corrosion preserves nanoparticle chemical stability.
Oxide-layer-treated nanoparticles will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the layer.
Oxide-layer-treated nanoparticles will exhibit better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the layer.
The proposed intervention is applicable throughout 773–1173 K.
The proposed stability benefit applies during exposure to both oxidative and reductive conditions.
The required oxide composition and thickness are not known.
A treated-versus-untreated thermal-exposure comparison using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and catalytic activity measurements can test the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is falsified if treated nanoparticles show lower stability or catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles.
